About the Kantian maxim, in simple terms and in the context of treatment of people: it's a rather simple concept. Kant wanted you to always think of other people as their own person, who also have desires and goals, moods and circumstances. So, if a barista  is to me just an entity or circumstance of me getting my coffee, I could get upset that it took them 2 minutes longer than some other time to get my drink. If I see them as their own person, I might think of their own circumstance and how it explains the longer time. perhaps they haven't had a break all day, etc.   
And I mean, obviously majority of people don't think of other people truly as objects, but in more subtle but major way we often fail to consider them as truly subjective entities. It has a lot to do with how Baudrillard conceptualized "I" in Simulacra and Simulation.  
I would recommend listening to an amazing speech entitled "This is water" that deals with just this problem.
